headline: Gmail “Send as” ends January 2027: a fix for Cloudflare Email Routing
author: Tom Baker

paragraphs.text: TBTom Baker27 November 2026, 14 minute read

The short answer: from January 2027, Gmail stops letting you send as addresses it does not host, and that includes any address on your own domain that Cloudflare Email Routing forwards to Gmail. Forwarding into Gmail keeps working, but your replies would go out from your @gmail.com address. To keep replying as you@yourdomain.com, send through Cloudflare Email Sending’s SMTP server from a desktop mail app, move the domain to a mailbox host, or use an inbox that runs in your own Cloudflare account.

I run more than twenty domains on Cloudflare, and for years my own setup was exactly the one this change breaks: catch-all forwarding into Gmail, and a “Send as” entry for every address I replied from. Below is what changes, what each way out costs, and the three traps I would want to know about before touching DNS.
Facts in this guide were checked against Google’s and Cloudflare’s own documentation on 27 November 2026. Sources are listed at the end.
What exactly changes in January 2027

Google is removing three features for addresses it does not host: “Send as” for third-party addresses in Gmail on the web and in the Gmail mobile apps, Gmailify, and fetching mail from other accounts over POP. Forwarding into Gmail, IMAP access to Gmail, and Send as for Gmail or Workspace addresses all keep working.
Google’s help page on the change is short and specific. The sentence that matters for Cloudflare users is this one:
You will no longer be able to send mail from third-party email accounts in Gmail on the web or in the Gmail mobile apps.
The Send as help page now carries the same warning at the top.
What stops working
• Send as for any address Gmail does not host.
• Gmailify, which applied Gmail’s spam filtering and labels to another provider’s account.
• Check mail from other accounts, Gmail’s POP fetch.
What keeps working
• Forwarding into Gmail. Google says plainly that you can keep auto-forwarding another provider’s mail to your Gmail address.
• IMAP and POP access to Gmail from Apple Mail, Outlook, Thunderbird and other clients.
• Send as for Google-hosted identities: other Gmail addresses, and aliases on a Google Workspace account.
• Mail you already have. Imported and received messages stay put.
The timeline
Your setup, before and after
Does this affect a domain on Cloudflare Email Routing?

Yes. Google keeps Send as only for “Google-hosted identities”. Cloudflare Email Routing only forwards mail; it does not host a mailbox, so an address it forwards is a third-party address to Gmail. That holds even if your Send as entry sends through smtp.gmail.com with an app password.
A lot of guides hedge on this. Google’s wording does not:

You can continue to use “Send as” for any Google-hosted identities, including other Gmail addresses or aliases associated with your Google Workspace account. The discontinuation will not impact these addresses, which only applies to third-party, non-Google email accounts.

If your domain’s MX records point at Cloudflare, Google does not host that address. The common Cloudflare Routing setup, where Send as uses smtp.gmail.com as its outgoing server, is still a third-party address in Gmail’s settings, and it is what goes away.

One more thing people try: the Gmail mobile app can still add non-Google accounts. That only helps if the other account has a mailbox the app can log in to over IMAP. Cloudflare Email Routing has no IMAP server, so there is nothing to add.
Your four options, compared

There are four realistic ways to keep replying from your domain: send through Cloudflare’s own SMTP server from a desktop mail app, move the domain’s mail to a mailbox host, switch to Google Workspace, or run an inbox inside your own Cloudflare account. They differ mostly in cost per domain and in how much setup each new address needs.

Prices are US list prices from each provider’s pricing page on 27 November 2026: Google Workspace ($7 a month per user on the annual plan, $8.40 flexible), Fastmail ($60 for 12 months), Migadu (Micro is $19 a year, yearly only), and iCloud+ ($0.99 a month for 50 GB in US dollar regions). Cloudflare’s side is covered in what Cloudflare Email Sending costs.
The small print on option B matters if you have many domains:
• Migadu Micro allows 200 incoming and 20 outgoing messages a day across the account, and its domain limit is “almost unlimited”.
• iCloud+ Custom Email Domain allows up to five domains with up to 10 addresses each, and needs an Apple Account with two-factor authentication.
• A domain’s MX records can only point one way. Moving to any host means Cloudflare Email Routing stops receiving for that domain.
Which one should you pick?
• One domain, you like Gmail, and you are happy to reply from a desktop app: option A. It is the smallest change.
• A few domains, and you want a phone app and IMAP: option B. Migadu Micro is the cheapest; Fastmail is the most polished.
• A team that already lives in Google Docs and Calendar: option C. It is the only option that keeps Send as inside Gmail itself.

• Many domains, catch-all on all of them, and a Mac: option D. Adding a domain costs nothing extra, and every address on it can reply as itself. I compare every app that does this in every inbox for Cloudflare Email Routing, compared.
Option A step by step: Apple Mail and Cloudflare’s SMTP server

Cloudflare Email Sending has an SMTP endpoint at smtp.mx.cloudflare.net, port 465, implicit TLS only. Onboard your domain for Email Sending, create an API token with the Email Sending: Edit permission, then add the server to your mail app with the username api_token and the token as the password.
Cloudflare added authenticated SMTP submission on 8 June 2026, as a beta, alongside the Workers binding and the REST API. It is the piece that makes option A possible without writing any code.
1. Onboard the domain for Email Sending
In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to Compute > Email Service > Email Sending, select Onboard Domain and pick the domain. Cloudflare adds these records:

MX cf-bounce.yourdomain.com route1.mx.cloudflare.net MX cf-bounce.yourdomain.com route2.mx.cloudflare.net MX cf-bounce.yourdomain.com route3.mx.cloudflare.net TXT cf-bounce.yourdomain.com "v=spf1 include:_spf.mx.cloudflare.net ~all" TXT cf-bounce._domainkey.yourdomain.com (DKIM public key) TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com (only if you have no DMARC record yet)
These live on the cf-bounce subdomain and sit alongside your Email Routing records on the root domain, so receiving is not affected. Read the DMARC trap below before you press Done.
2. Create the API token
Create a Cloudflare API token with the Email Sending: Edit permission. Cloudflare accepts account-owned tokens, which it recommends, and user-owned ones.

Treat it like a password. Cloudflare’s SMTP reference is explicit: anyone with the token can send email from any onboarded domain on the account. If you onboard twenty domains, one leaked token can send as all twenty.
3. Test it before you touch your mail app
This is the test from Cloudflare’s docs. Swap in your token and two addresses:

cat > mail.txt <<'MAIL' From: you@yourdomain.com To: you@gmail.com Subject: Cloudflare SMTP test Sent through smtp.mx.cloudflare.net. MAIL curl --ssl-reqd \ --url "smtps://smtp.mx.cloudflare.net:465" \ --user "api_token:<API_TOKEN>" \ --mail-from "you@yourdomain.com" \ --mail-rcpt "you@gmail.com" \ --upload-file mail.txt
On the Workers Free plan this only works if the recipient is a verified destination address in your account. Anything else is refused at RCPT TO with 550 5.7.1. Sending to anyone needs Workers Paid.
4. Apple Mail settings

In Mail, open Settings > Accounts, choose the account you read your forwarded mail in, open Server Settings, and choose Edit SMTP Server List from the Outgoing Mail Account menu. Add a server and turn off Automatically manage connection settings.

Then add your domain addresses to the account. In Account Information, open the Email Address menu and choose Edit Email Addresses to list every address you want in the From menu. Check the From address before you send a reply.
Cloudflare does not offer port 587 with STARTTLS, or port 25, for sending. If Mail says the server is unavailable, the TLS setting is the first thing to check.
5. The Apple Mail catch

Apple Mail sends everything from an account through that account’s one outgoing server. If the account is your Gmail account and you point it at Cloudflare, mail from your @gmail.com address goes to Cloudflare too, and Cloudflare refuses it with 550 5.7.1 Sender denied, because gmail.com is not a domain you onboarded.
Two ways round it:
• Send only domain mail from that account, and send personal Gmail from the Gmail website or app.
• Use Thunderbird, which lets each identity have its own outgoing server.
Thunderbird, and catch-all addresses

Thunderbird handles this better. Add the Cloudflare server under Outgoing Server (SMTP) with the same values: port 465, connection security SSL/TLS, authentication Normal password, username api_token. Then create an identity for your domain and give it that server.

If you use catch-all, open the identity’s settings and set Reply from this identity when delivery headers match to *@yourdomain.com. A reply to mail sent to an address you never created will then go out from that address, not your default one. Apple Mail has no equivalent; you can only reply from addresses you have listed.
Three traps nobody mentions

Onboarding Email Sending adds a DMARC record with a p=reject policy if your domain has none, which can make your existing Gmail Send as replies bounce. Cloudflare’s Email preview stores the content of what you send for about seven days, on by default. And Email Sending is a beta product that Cloudflare describes as transactional only.
1. The DMARC record Cloudflare adds

When you onboard a domain for Email Sending, Cloudflare adds a DMARC record on _dmarc.yourdomain.com only if the domain has none, and its default policy is p=reject. Cloudflare’s own advice is to keep p=reject only if Email Service is the only thing sending for the domain, and to use p=none while other services still send.

Gmail Send as is one of those other services. A reply sent through smtp.gmail.com as you@yourdomain.com is signed by Gmail, not by your domain, so it does not pass DMARC for your domain. With p=reject in place, receivers are told to refuse it.
So during the switch:
• Check whether you already have a record: dig +short TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com
• If Cloudflare adds one, change it to p=none in DNS > Records while Gmail Send as still sends anything. Cloudflare does not lock it or overwrite your edit.
• Move to p=quarantine, then p=reject, once Gmail is no longer sending as the domain.
2. Email preview keeps a copy of what you send

Email Sending has an Email preview setting that stores sent messages so you can read them in the Activity log. Previews are kept for about seven days, and new sending domains have it turned on automatically.

For an app sending password resets, that is a handy debugging tool. For personal replies to customers, lawyers or your accountant, it means the full text of what you sent can be read in your Cloudflare dashboard by anyone with access to it for a week. To turn it off, go to Email Sending, select the domain, open Settings and switch off Enable email preview.
3. It is a beta, and Cloudflare calls it transactional

Cloudflare’s docs label Email Sending Beta, and its FAQ says Email Service “supports transactional email only”, in answer to a question about marketing mail. One person replying to the people who wrote to them is not marketing. But it is a different use from the order confirmations Cloudflare’s examples are built around, and I would rather say that plainly than pretend otherwise.

The practical limits are covered in the routing and sending limits: 50 recipients per message, 25 MiB per message, and a daily quota that Cloudflare does not publish and that starts conservative on new accounts.
What it costs to reply through Cloudflare

Replying through Cloudflare Email Sending needs the Workers Paid plan: $5 a month for the whole Cloudflare account, with 3,000 outbound emails a month included and $0.35 per 1,000 after that. A person replying from any number of domains will almost always pay just the $5, or $60 a year.

The 3,000 is per account, not per domain, and it resets with your billing cycle. Receiving through Email Routing stays free and unlimited on every plan, according to Cloudflare’s pricing page. If your account already pays for Workers Paid for something else, replying costs nothing extra until you pass 3,000 a month.
For the full table of what each option costs over three years, including Workspace and Fastmail, see the cheapest way to get email on multiple domains.
Migration checklist before January
• List every Send as address in Gmail under Settings > Accounts and Import. Note which domain each belongs to.
• List your Cloudflare routing rules, including any catch-all. Addresses you reply from under a catch-all will not appear in Gmail’s list, so check your Sent folder too.
• Pick a path from the four options above, per domain if you need to.
• Set up sending authentication for the new path: onboard the domain for Email Sending, or add the new host’s SPF and DKIM records.
• Check DMARC before and after onboarding, and set p=none while Gmail still sends as the domain.
• Send test replies to a Gmail, an Outlook.com and an iCloud address. Open the original message in each and check that SPF, DKIM and DMARC pass for your domain.
• Remove the old Send as entries once replies go out the new way, then tighten DMARC and update your signatures.
Where EmailFast fits

I make EmailFast, which is option D. It is a Mac app that receives every address on every domain through Cloudflare Email Routing with catch-all, keeps the mail in a small mailbox in your own Cloudflare account, and replies from whichever address each message was sent to through Cloudflare Email Sending. There is no Gmail in the loop, so the January change does not touch it.

It sets up the records, routing and sending for each domain you tick, and incoming mail is sealed on arrival with a key only your Macs hold. You can see exactly what it creates in your account and how the sealing works. It is $129 once, plus Cloudflare’s Workers Paid plan if your account does not have it. It is in beta at the moment.
If you are happy in Gmail with one domain, option A is enough. If you have twenty domains and a catch-all on each, that is the problem I built it for.
